column7: Inverted: `selectSkillSlashCommands` treats the explicit command names as `takenNames` and drops the skill from the `/` menu, so `commands/review.md` shadows a `review` skill. The module comment states the opposite rule deliberately ("Explicit commands are authored for this purpose and are the more specific declaration").
column9: All three checks confirm the finding, and a fourth corroborates it. (1) VERBATIM: curl of https://code.claude.com/docs/en/claude-directory.md line 293 carries the tip array element exactly as quoted: 'If a skill and command share a name, the skill takes precedence'. Reading the whole line, the two sibling tips ($ARGUMENTS usage; 'New commands should usually be skills instead; commands remain supported') do not qualify or reverse it. The page is row 77 of scripts/claude-doc-pages.tsv, so it is a valid Claude Code contract page. Independently corroborated on a second page: code.claude.com/docs/en/skills.md and .../slash-commands.md both carry, at line 122, 'If you have files in `.claude/commands/`, those work the same way, but if a skill and a command share the same name, the skill takes precedence.' (2) CODE: packages/shared/src/slash-commands/custom-commands.ts:444 is literally `if (taken.has(skill.logicalName)) continue;`, and the JSDoc at :425-433 states the inverted rule on purpose: '`takenNames` wins: when an explicit command file already provides `/review`, the skill does not also claim that bare name. Explicit commands are authored for this purpose and are the more specific declaration.' (3) CONSEQUENCE, verified separately from the identifier and in the right subsystem: SessionManager.skillSlashCommands (packages/server-core/src/sessions/SessionManager.ts:16006-16014) forwards takenNames, and BOTH call sites pass `nativeCommands.map(command => command.name)` — the listing path :16039 and the resolution path :16120. `nativeCommands` is loadSessionCustomSlashCommands (:15837), which is discoverCustomSlashCommands over the real .claude/commands/*.md files (plus workflow recipes) — not built-in/native CLI commands, so this is the correct subsystem and not a name collision with a sibling. Nothing upstream reverses it: listCustomSlashCommandSummaries returns [...native, ...plugin, ...skills, ...mcp] with `native` unconditional, the shadowed skill is dropped before the push so it contributes NO entry at all, skillSlashCommandId/`custom:skill:` has no other producer anywhere in packages/ or apps/, and the renderer (AppShell.tsx:1408) only displays the server-supplied list without re-deduping. The behaviour is pinned by tests: custom-commands.test.ts:172-178 asserts `selectSkillSlashCommands([skill('review'), skill('audit')], ['review'])` yields only 'audit', with the comment 'Precedence: an explicit command file wins'. (4) NOT an owner decision: it is not among the nine dated entries in docs/superpowers/specs/2026-07-29-inert-worklist.md section 3 (seatbelt wildcard, availableModels/isManagedModelAllowed, autoMode.classifyAllShell, ManagedDeliveryStateV1.drops, hooks-runtime.ts, SdkMcpServerConfig.required, SessionMirrorStore.delete, MirrorSessionKey.subpath, listSessionSummaries), nor in section 4's false positives, and grep finds nothing in the parity audit or the deviation register. It is also not a Nessy product difference (no branding, gateway, or dropped-subscription angle). The only prior record is docs/superpowers/plans/2026-07-26-skills-invocation.md, which at :427-429 explicitly delegated the choice to the executor ('Decide the precedence between an explicit custom command and a skill-derived one, and state it in the commit body') without citing Claude's docs; tracker row 5 (:568, commit 94cb0f9c) then recorded the chosen direction. That is an undocumented executor choice made against an unread contract, not a reasoned deviation from a known one.

column5: Skills accept arguments: <C>/deploy staging</C> passes "staging" as <C>$ARGUMENTS</C>. Use <C>$0</C>, <C>$1</C>, and so on for positional access
column6: Command and skill bodies expand positional argument placeholders `$0`, `$1`, … in addition to `$ARGUMENTS`.
column7: Split. Runtime SKILL content does expand `$0`/`$1` (quote-aware, with escape rules). Custom slash commands — `.nessy-agent/commands/*.md`, `.agents/commands/*.md`, and plugin prompt-commands — do not: the substitution is a single regex over `$ARGUMENTS|{{args}}`, so `/fix-issue 123` leaves a literal `$0` in the prompt.
column9: All three legs confirm. (1) QUOTE VERBATIM: claude-directory.md line 222 reads exactly `tips: [<>Skills accept arguments: <C>/deploy staging</C> passes "staging" as <C>$ARGUMENTS</C>. Use <C>$0</C>, <C>$1</C>, and so on for positional access</>, ...]`. Read the whole line: the rest of the tips array is about `description` frontmatter and bundled reference docs, and reverses nothing. The quoted sentence is about SKILLS, and our skills half COMPLIES -- but the SAME PAGE states the identical rule for commands at line 304: `<C>$ARGUMENTS</C> substitutes whatever you typed after the command name. For positional access, use <C>$0</C> <C>$1</C> and so on.` (in the `.claude/commands/fix-issue.md` example block, alongside line 293's `Use <C>$ARGUMENTS</C> in the file to accept parameters: <C>/fix-issue 123</C>`). Line 293's second clause -- 'New commands should usually be skills instead; commands remain supported' -- confirms commands are still a live contract, not deprecated away. So the divergence is doc-grounded on this page, just anchored to the wrong sentence of it. (2) CITED LINE EXACT: packages/server-core/src/handlers/rpc/sessions.ts:334 is verbatim `modelMessage = command.body.replace(/\$ARGUMENTS|\{\{args\}\}/g, () => args)`, with the comment at :329-332 stating the pass substitutes ONLY those two tokens. (3) CONSEQUENCE VERIFIED SEPARATELY FROM THE IDENTIFIER, one layer up and one down. Up: `modelMessage` is passed as the 11th argument of `sessionManager.sendMessage` at sessions.ts:373, i.e. it IS the model-facing body -- nothing downstream re-expands it. Down: `resolveCustomSlashCommand` (SessionManager.ts:16080-16179) returns `body` unmodified for every non-MCP source (native from `parseCustomCommand`; plugin prompt-command from `materializer.readText` at :16165; workflow from `workflowSlashCommandBody`, which is literally `[workflow:<name>]\n$ARGUMENTS`; skill from `skillSlashCommandBody`, `[skill:<ref>] $ARGUMENTS`). Repo-wide there is exactly one other `$ARGUMENTS` replacer, SessionManager.ts:481, and it is a DIFFERENT subsystem (prompt-hook input JSON) -- named explicitly so the sibling-subsystem trap is excluded. So `/fix-issue 123` on a `.nessy-agent/commands/fix-issue.md` body containing `$1` reaches the model with a literal `$1`. POSITIVE CONTROL for the split, both directions: the skills expander `expandSkillArguments`/`matchArgumentPlaceholder` (packages/shared/src/capabilities/runtime-skill-content.ts:497-600) implements the full family -- `$ARGUMENTS[N]` (:508), `$ARGUMENTS` (:518), `$name` (:527-538), bare `$N` (:539-548, `values[Number(...)]`, undefined stays literal per skills.md:323) plus backslash escaping (:577-585) -- and it is reached for a skill slash command because sessions.ts:334 turns `[skill:x] $ARGUMENTS` into `[skill:x] staging`, `runtimeSkillArguments` (:607-617) slices the tail off the marker, and base-agent.ts:2329 feeds it to `materializeRuntimeSkillInvocation` as `argumentsText`. And the fork positively KNOWS commands lack this: packages/shared/src/plugins/format-adapters/claude.ts:653-654 defines `DYNAMIC_SUBSTITUTION_PATTERNS` with `{ pattern: /\$[1-9]\b/, kind: 'positional-argument' }`, used at :741-749 to push a `plugin.deferred.claude_command_dynamic_substitution` entry with the comment 'Never evaluate shell/file expressions -- only detect and defer them'. Detect-and-defer is the opposite of expand. NOT one of the nine dated owner decisions in 2026-07-29-inert-worklist.md section 3 (SEATBELT_TESTING_WILDCARD, availableModels/enforceAvailableModels, autoMode.classifyAllShell, ManagedDeliveryStateV1.drops, plugins/hooks-runtime.ts, SdkMcpServerConfig.required, SessionMirrorStore.delete, MirrorSessionKey.subpath/listSubkeys, listSessionSummaries/listSessions) -- section 3 has zero hits for 'positional' or '$ARGUMENTS'. Not a de-brand or dropped-provider difference either: this is Nessy's own custom-command surface, not a Claude/ChatGPT subscription flow. The one imprecision worth recording is the anchoring -- the finding quotes the skills sentence, which we satisfy, while the actual gap is the commands sentence on the same page.

'')))`, returning a single `{ message: invocation.slice(command.label.length).trim(), customSlashCommandId: command.id }`. Input `/skill-a /skill-b do XYZ` against commands built by the production `skillSlashCommandId`:    SUBMISSION    {"message":"/skill-b do XYZ","customSlashCommandId":"custom:skill:skill-a"}   MODEL MESSAGE "[skill:skill-a] /skill-b do XYZ"   REFS          ["skill-a"]   CONTROL REFS  ["skill-a","skill-b"]  The MODEL MESSAGE line reproduces the server substitution exactly as `rpc/sessions.ts:335` performs it (`command.body.replace(/\$ARGUMENTS|\{\{args\}\}/g, () => args)`) over the production body from `slash-commands/custom-commands.ts:302-304`, `skillSlashCommandBody(reference) => `[skill:${reference}] $ARGUMENTS``. (1) The cited line is a DIFFERENT SUBSYSTEM. packages/server-core/src/bootstrap/plugin-runtime-dependencies.ts:238 sits inside `runDependencyInstallerWithQuota`, and `invocation` there comes from `buildPluginRuntimeDependencyInstallInvocation(bunPath, directory, hostEnvironment, frozenLockfile)` (:44-89, command = bunPath, args = bun install flags with a sandboxed HOME/TMPDIR/cache). It spawns the PLUGIN RUNTIME DEPENDENCY INSTALLER under a quota watchdog. It has nothing to do with stdio MCP servers; the finding named the wrong subsystem. (2) 'Subprocesses are spawned directly ... spawns stdio MCP servers' is FALSE. packages/shared/src/mcp/client.ts:724, in SupervisedStdioClientTransport.startProcess, starts every stdio MCP server through `this.authority.processSupervisor.start({ ... semanticId: 'plugin-mcp-stdio' ... })`, and ProcessSupervisor spawns the ISOLATION-REWRITTEN argv `plan?.command ?? request.command` / `plan?.args ?? args` at packages/server-core/src/pi-harness/process-supervisor.ts:244, behind a `beforeStart` admission gate. A launcher-prefix chokepoint therefore exists and is live: packages/session-tools-core/src/runtime/trusted-isolation-launchers.ts:23 `resolveTrustedIsolationLauncher` resolves absolute host-owned launcher paths (sandbox-exec/bwrap/firejail/unshare) from a fixed allowlist that deliberately never consults PATH, and filesystem-/network-isolation build the prefixed argv the supervisor then spawns. (3) Even had stdio MCP been spawned raw, it would be evidence for a DIFFERENT page. The same doc, line 137 (section 'Relationship to CLAUDE_CODE_SHELL_PREFIX'), states that CLAUDE_CODE_PROCESS_WRAPPER wraps Claude Code's own processes while CLAUDE_CODE_SHELL_PREFIX wraps 'the shell commands Claude runs on your behalf, such as Bash tool calls, hooks, and the commands that start stdio MCP servers', and that 'a launcher written for one doesn't work as the other'. Lines 23-30 scope the launcher to the on-demand background service, agent-view terminal hosts and warm-standby sessions, post-update self-relaunches, Remote Control workers, and tmux/iTerm2 teammate panes - the CLI's supervisor architecture. Nessy Desktop is an Electron app with none of it: the post-update restart is electron-updater's `quitAndInstall` (apps/electron/src/main/auto-update.ts:14, 'quitAndInstall() handles restart natively - no external scripts'), performed by the OS installer rather than a self-spawn from our own binary; subagents and workflows are IN-PROCESS child sessions via `spawnChildSession` (orchestrator/spawner.ts, called at subtask.ts:95, workflow-tool.ts:358 and :390, review-tool.ts:309, guardian-runner.ts:71), so there is no OS process to prefix. column9: Quote verified verbatim at debug-your-config.md:72 ('If /hooks shows the hook but it still does not fire, the next step is to watch hook evaluation live. Start a session with `claude --debug hooks` and trigger the tool call. The debug log records each event, which matchers were checked, and the hook's exit code and output.'); the rest of the line does not reverse it, and :56 ('claude --debug mcp') and :122 corroborate the category form. This fork DOES ship a `--debug` flag; it lives on the process that actually runs sessions, hooks and MCP — the Electron desktop host — not on the thin websocket client the finding cited. apps/electron/src/main/logger.ts:16 `if (process.argv.includes('--debug')) return true` feeds `isDebugMode` (:31), and apps/electron/src/main/index.ts:93-97 turns it into `NESSY_DEBUG=1` + `enableDebug()` + `setPerfEnabled(true)`. So 'no --debug flag at all' is true only of apps/cli, and false of the product — exactly the sibling-subsystem shape AGENTS.md warns about. (2) CONSEQUENCE IS FALSE SEPARATELY. The live hook-evaluation logging the flag exists to enable is present: packages/shared/src/automations/automation-system.ts logs the lifecycle-hook sources loaded (:237), disableAllHooks (:229), the action count (:257), the events emitted per session (:560) and webhook failures (:795), all gated behind isDebugEnabled(); and packages/shared/src/automations/event-logger.ts keeps an append-only events.jsonl recording every automation event with its ActionExecutionResult[] and duration, independent of any flag. apps/cli/src/server-spawner.ts:75 exists precisely to surface these — 'Pipe server stderr to our stderr so --debug logs are visible (unless quiet)' — exposed through the CLI's own `--verbose`/`-v` (index.ts:120-122, :881, help at :2082). `NESSY_DEBUG=1 nessy-general-agent run … --verbose` is the CLI's route to the same log. Not an inert-worklist section 3 owner decision and not a branding/subscription/gateway product difference; refuted on scope and consequence, not on category.

column5: A deep link never executes anything on its own. The link only chooses a directory and fills the prompt box.
column6: The handler accepts exactly one path (`open`), and a deep link can only choose a directory and pre-fill the prompt box — nothing is sent or executed until the user presses Enter.
column7: `nessy://action/new-session?input=…&send=true` sends the prompt straight to the model with no user confirmation — `const shouldSend = parsed.params.send === 'true'` then `window.electronAPI.sendMessage(session.id, parsed.params.input!, …)`. The scheme is registered OS-wide via `app.setAsDefaultProtocolClient(DEEPLINK_SCHEME)` (`apps/electron/src/main/index.ts:197`), and the same handler also routes `delete-session/{id}`, `flag-session/{id}`, `rename-session` and `oauth` (`apps/electron/src/main/deep-link.ts:22-24`), so a link on any web page reaches them. There is no external-origin gate and no `Prompt from an external link` warning line.
column9: All three checks pass. (1) The quoted sentence is verbatim at deep-links.md:39, and the WHOLE line reinforces rather than reverses it: 'A deep link never executes anything on its own. The link only chooses a directory and fills the prompt box. If you click a link from a page you do not trust, the prompt is still inert: nothing reaches the model until you read what was filled in and press Enter.' Line 45 independently confirms the one-path claim ('Every deep link starts with claude-cli://open, which is the only path the handler accepts') and line 41 confirms the 'Prompt from an external link' warning line. (2) The cited file:line is exact: apps/electron/src/renderer/contexts/NavigationContext.tsx:754 is `const shouldSend = parsed.params.send === 'true'`, inside `case 'new-session':` opened at :677, and :755-763 calls window.electronAPI.sendMessage(session.id, parsed.params.input!, ...) behind a 100 ms setTimeout. apps/electron/src/main/index.ts:197 is app.setAsDefaultProtocolClient(DEEPLINK_SCHEME) as claimed. (3) The CONSEQUENCE was verified separately from the identifier, and the external path is real and ungated end-to-end: app.on('open-url') at index.ts:~240 calls handleDeepLink unconditionally with no origin classification (the classifyExternalUrl/'dangerous' gate in main/handlers/system.ts:206-215 sits only on the renderer->main shell:openUrl IPC, not on the OS path); deep-link.ts:185-190 copies every query param except `window` and `sidebar`, so `send` survives; handleDeepLink:334-338 pushes DeepLinkNavigation to the renderer; the listener at NavigationContext.tsx:1096-1123 re-serialises actionParams back into an `action/...` route and calls navigate(); navigate() at :841 dispatches parsed.type === 'action' to handleActionNavigation at :861. No trust prompt, no origin check and no 'external link' warning string exists anywhere in apps/electron/src or the i18n bundles (grep -ani, no hits). The sibling-subsystem trap does not apply: `send=true` exists because the app uses this scheme as its own in-app command bus (new-session-deep-link.ts:25-26 'auto-sends the seeded prompt', called only from EditPopover.tsx:1089), but the same handler is registered OS-wide with no distinction between the internal caller and a web page, so the internal design intent does not bound the external surface. Not an owner decision: all nine dated decisions in 2026-07-29-inert-worklist.md section 3 were read (seatbelt wildcard, availableModels/isManagedModelAllowed, autoMode.classifyAllShell, ManagedDeliveryStateV1.drops, hooks-runtime.ts, SdkMcpServerConfig.required, SessionMirrorStore.delete, MirrorSessionKey.subpath, listSessionSummaries) and none concerns deep links. Not a deliberate product difference either: only the scheme name (craft:// -> nessy://) is rebrand; auto-send and the destructive action routes are substantive behaviour. The existing records treat the page as OPEN, not decided: coverage-map row 97 marks deep-links yellow with 'Контракт не снят', and the parity audit at :1719 files deep links under 'Minor, no row, listed for completeness' — a title-level triage the audit itself says was 'not enough to audit field by field'.

column9: Doc half checks out; the consequence does not. (1) QUOTE VERBATIM: deep-links.md:163 reads exactly 'To prevent registration entirely, set [`disableDeepLinkRegistration`](/docs/en/settings) to `"disable"` in `settings.json`.' The rest of that two-sentence line only adds managed-settings enforcement, so it does not reverse the claim. (2) CITED LINE ACCURATE: apps/electron/src/main/index.ts:190-198 calls app.setAsDefaultProtocolClient(DEEPLINK_SCHEME) unconditionally (:193 dev branch, :197 production) with no setting consulted; `grep -ran disableDeepLinkRegistration` over the repo hits only the doc-sweep JSON/markdown artifacts, never code; MANAGED_PI_POLICY_KEYS (packages/shared/src/agent/pi-harness/managed-policy.ts:501-534) carries no equivalent. (3) CONSEQUENCE FALSE ON THREE COUNTS. (a) WRONG SUBSYSTEM. Claude's key gates the CLI, which lazily writes a user-level handler (~/Applications/Claude Code URL Handler.app, a .desktop file, HKCU\Software\Classes\claude-cli) when you send your first interactive prompt (deep-links.md:153-159). Nessy has no CLI-side handler at all: setAsDefaultProtocolClient appears only in the Electron main process (one src hit, plus its build output in apps/electron/dist/main.cjs); apps/cli registers nothing. The GUI's scheme is declared STATICALLY in the bundle -- apps/electron/electron-builder.yml:82-84 `protocols: - name: Nessy Desktop / schemes: [nessy]` -- which electron-builder turns into CFBundleURLTypes in Info.plist, NSIS registry entries on Windows, and MimeType=x-scheme-handler/nessy on Linux. (b) THE IMPLIED REMEDY WOULD NOT WORK. Gating index.ts:193/197 on a setting cannot 'prevent registration entirely': LaunchServices and the installer have already registered the scheme from the installed bundle, and setAsDefaultProtocolClient only selects the DEFAULT handler among claimants. So this is not the missing off-switch for the auto-send finding -- flipping it off would leave nessy:// still routed to the app. (c) THE SCHEME IS LOAD-BEARING HERE, UNLIKE CLAUDE'S. nessy://auth-callback / nessy://auth-complete is the OAuth redirect target (packages/shared/src/auth/callback-server.ts:41; carved out at apps/electron/src/main/deep-link.ts:111-114 and packages/server-core/src/handlers/rpc/system.ts:83), and nessy:// doubles as the app's INTERNAL navigation transport (system.ts:283-312 routes internal nessy:// links over RPC without ever touching the OS). Claude's claude-cli:// carries only the optional launch-a-terminal convenience, so switching it off costs nothing there; a key with Claude's exact semantics would break sign-in in this fork. Also a deliberate product-shape difference: Nessy Desktop is an Electron GUI, not a terminal CLI, so the feature the setting exists to disable -- click a link, a terminal emulator opens with a pre-filled prompt -- does not exist to be disabled. Not one of the nine dated owner decisions in 2026-07-29-inert-worklist.md section 3.

Our Browser pane ships a single `browser_tool` whose `navigate` subcommand takes a bare URL and starts nothing — there is no dev-server start/stop, no auto-verify-after-edit, and no port-conflict policy.
column9: All three factual checks pass, but the finding is refuted as a divergence because it is an already-recorded product/scope decision in the parity audit itself. (1) QUOTE VERBATIM: desktop.md line 428 contains the claimed sentence exactly (python substring check True). The whole line has two more sentences ('Preview uses this folder as its working directory, so if you selected a parent folder, subfolders with their own dev servers won't be detected automatically. To work with a subfolder's server, either start a session in that folder directly or add a configuration manually.') — they narrow scope to the session folder, they do not reverse the conclusion. The doc's field table (475-486), autoVerify default (450-452), autoPort tri-state (539-543), PORT hand-off (545) and the localhost origin-only/matching-port rule (517) all check out, so the CLAIMED BEHAVIOUR is a faithful reading of the page. (2) CITED LINE: packages/shared/src/agent/browser-tool-runtime.ts:741 is `if (cmd === 'navigate') {`, whose body takes `parts.slice(1).join(' ').trim()` as a bare URL and calls `fns.navigate(url)` — it starts nothing. Correct as cited. (3) ABSENCE, NUL-SAFE: `grep -rna -a` for launch\.json|autoVerify|autoPort|runtimeExecutable over packages, apps, scripts, docs-site returns zero. The browser tool exposes 32 subcommands (open, navigate, snapshot, find, click, click-at, drag, fill, type, select, upload, set-clipboard, get-clipboard, paste, screenshot, screenshot-region, console, window-resize, network, wait, key, downloads, scroll, back, forward, evaluate, focus, windows, release, close, hide) — none starts, stops, port-checks or auto-verifies a server. ONE LAYER UP/DOWN: the only `.claude/launch.json` in the tree is the repo's own at the root, consumed by the Claude Code harness (my own preview_start tool), not by our product — the claim already says this and it is right. The only 'dev server' hits in product source are apps/electron/src/main/window-manager.ts:114/287/340/380 and apps/viewer/vite.config.ts:30, which are the app shell's OWN Vite dev server for hot reload — an identically-worded sibling subsystem, not a user-project preview server. No upstream layer supplies the consequence. Not one of the nine inert-worklist section 3 owner decisions. REFUTATION: docs/superpowers/specs/2026-07-25-nessy-claude-parity-audit.md — the named source of truth — already rules on this at section 5e-2, lines 1719-1726: 'Minor, no row, listed for completeness: ... and the desktop product surfaces (preview servers, PR status, diff view, integrated terminal) that are product decisions rather than loop parity.' column9: Quote is verbatim (desktop.md:719, whole line read; the second sentence only tightens the type rule to JSON boolean true, it does not reverse anything). The identifier half of the finding is also true: managed-policy.ts:501 is `export const MANAGED_PI_POLICY_KEYS = [` and neither `disableBrowserExternalNavigation` nor `browserExternalPageTools` appears in it, and `grep -ran` for both names over the repo hits only docs/spec/JSON sweep files. A managed `permissionDsl` deny rule is the documented real boundary and it reaches `browser_tool`. managed-policy.ts:298-301 states it in so many words ('An admin who needs a real boundary uses a managed `permissionDsl` deny rule, which our deterministic gate applies BEFORE the judge is consulted at all'); mode-manager.ts:2103-2117 runs `deniedToolPatterns`/`disallowedTools` and 2129 runs `toolRules` deny BEFORE the ALWAYS_ALLOWED_TOOLS set that contains 'browser_tool' (mode-manager.ts:2001), and the comment at 2010-2013 names the deny check as 'the lever'; pi-agent.ts:1729-1760 applies `filterCapabilityIdentitiesByWholeToolDeny`, which removes a whole-tool-denied binding from the exposed tool set, and `browser_tool` is a static binding (harness-tool-descriptor.ts:160, :293). (2) A second off-switch exists one layer down: `getBrowserToolEnabled()` (config/storage.ts:1053) gates `mcp__session__browser_tool` out of the session tool defs at pi-agent.ts:1610-1612, defaulting from the bundled `apps/electron/resources/config-defaults.json` (`browserToolEnabled`, storage.ts:91/179), so a corporate build can ship it off. (3) The evidence's own count is wrong: MANAGED_PI_POLICY_KEYS holds 32 keys, not 34 (counted programmatically). (4) Scope: the `desktop` page already carries a recorded verdict in docs/superpowers/specs/2026-07-31-claude-coverage-map.md row 98 -- U+2B1C 'vne produkta, verdikt zapisan', note 'chuzhoy desktop-produkt'. column5: | `managedMcpServers`                        | push MCP server configurations to all users in a third-party deployment. Each entry specifies a transport of `"http"`, `"sse"`, or `"stdio"`, connection details, and optionally a `toolPolicy` map that restricts which tools in that server users can invoke.
column6: `managedMcpServers` pushes MCP server configurations to all users, each entry naming a transport of `"http"`, `"sse"` or `"stdio"` plus an optional per-server `toolPolicy` map, and is the documented delivery path for third-party deployments that receive no admin-console settings.
column7: Our managed policy can only restrict — `allowedMcpServers` / `deniedMcpServers` (`managed-policy.ts:129-130`) — never push a server definition, and carries no per-server tool restriction. `grep -a managedMcpServers` across the repo hits only the docs spec. Our fork is precisely the third-party deployment shape the key exists for.
column9: Legs 1 and 2 hold; leg 3 fails, and the finding's own OUR STATE carries a false half. (1) QUOTE - VERBATIM but TRUNCATED at the load-bearing clause. `curl -sL https://code.claude.com/docs/en/desktop.md` (960 lines), line 722, in the `### Managed settings` table, contains the claimed text as an exact substring. Reading the WHOLE line, two sentences were cut: 'Available in third-party (3P) Desktop deployments only. Deliver this key through the managed settings file or MDM, since third-party deployments do not receive admin-console settings.' The second cut sentence is the one the finding paraphrases into its claim; the FIRST is the one it drops, and it is the scope limit - the key exists only in third-party deployments of Claude Desktop, i.e. Anthropic's own app shipped into a fleet whose deployer is not Anthropic. Nessy is not a Claude Desktop deployment: it is a separate application whose vendor and deployer are the same organization, so the vendor/administrator separation the MDM push channel bridges does not exist here. 'Our fork is precisely the third-party deployment shape the key exists for' is the finding's own inference, not the page's. (2) CITATIONS - ACCURATE. `managed-policy.ts:129-130` are exactly `readonly allowedMcpServers?: readonly ManagedMcpEntryV1[]` / `readonly deniedMcpServers?: readonly ManagedMcpEntryV1[]`; `:501` is `export const MANAGED_PI_POLICY_KEYS = [`, whose 30-key list contains no MCP-server-definition key. The absence is real: `grep -ran managedMcpServers` over the whole tree (with -a) hits only doc/spec files - `2026-07-26-r-queue-doc-verification.md:698`, the sweep TSV/JSON, and this row. `toolPolicy` appears once in product code, as the type of an unused `RuntimeMcpServer.toolPolicy` field (`capabilities/resolver.ts:316`, interface at `:133`), with no producer or consumer. (3) CONSEQUENCE - HALF FALSE. OUR STATE asserts the managed policy 'carries no per-server tool restriction'. It does. The same admin-only file the MCP lists arrive in - `/Library/Application Support/Nessy/managed-policy.json`, `/etc/nessy/managed-policy.json`, `%ProgramData%\Nessy\managed-policy.json` (`server-core/src/pi-harness/managed-policy-loader.ts:48-50`), plus a `managed-policy.d/` drop-in dir - carries `permissionDsl` (`managed-policy.ts:82`, key at `:504`) and `claudeRules`, and that DSL has a first-class `mcp` matcher: `permission-dsl.ts:946-950` splits a tool's `permissionName` on `__` and wildcard-matches SERVER and TOOL independently, so `mcp__jira__delete_*` is exactly 'restrict which tools in that server users can invoke'. `claude-permission-rules.ts:171` parses the `mcp__server__tool` spelling from managed `claudeRules` too. It is enforced, not parsed-and-dropped: `SessionManager.ts:4095-4096` passes `managedPermissionDsl` into the turn, `:14267`/`:16245` read it again, the shipped docblock at `managed-policy.ts:299-301` names it as THE admin boundary ('a managed `permissionDsl` deny rule, which our deterministic gate applies BEFORE the judge is consulted at all'), and `isWholeToolDenyForIdentity` additionally REMOVES a wholly-denied MCP tool from the model's context. So the per-server tool-restriction half of the divergence is simply not a gap. (4) The remaining half - no managed key that PUSHES a server definition - is true, but it is (a) already recorded, not undiscovered, and (b) met differently by this fork's deployment shape. Recorded: `docs/architecture/managed-mcp-access.md:91` files the `managed-mcp.json` fixed deployment as 'documented, not implemented - a separate deployment channel', and the sibling finding f039, on that same absence, was already refuted 2026-08-02. Met differently: the fork ships the corporate server set IN THE PRODUCT - `BUILTIN_DP_MCP_SERVERS` (`packages/shared/src/mcp/builtin-dp-servers.ts:111`) is 29 frozen `dp ai mcp` server definitions (dpGitlab, dpJira, dpSage, SpiritK8s, ...) delivered to every user of the deployment, each with a `defaultEnabled` and a per-server user toggle (`config/builtin-dp-mcp-settings.ts`, `builtin-dp-mcp-preferences.ts`). 'Every user in this deployment gets these servers' is answered at build time because there is one organization, one gateway and one builder - which is the same de-brand/corporate-target difference that removes the admin console, the claude.ai connectors and the MDM fleet from this product. Not one of the nine dated owner decisions in `2026-07-29-inert-worklist.md` section 3 - I read all nine; none concerns MCP deployment.

column5: Claude can't send cross-session messages from a session nobody is watching, such as a scheduled-task run, and can't deliver messages into one.
column6: Cross-session messaging is gated on whether a human is watching: an unattended run can neither send nor receive one.
column7: `handleSendAgentMessage` validates only that the target id is non-empty and is not the caller's own session; there is no attended/unattended check on either the sender or the recipient. `grep -a "unattended\|isWatched\|attended"` over `packages/session-tools-core/src` returns nothing. Our `SchedulerTick` automations create exactly the unwatched sessions the rule exists for, and they carry the tool. The sender-envelope and 20-session-default halves of the same section do match (`tool-defs.ts:839`, `send-agent-message.ts:35-41`).
column9: Doc sentence verified verbatim: desktop.md line 362, third bullet of the 'Claude Code applies three safety behaviors across sessions' list, single sentence, no reversing second half. Cited file:line verified: packages/session-tools-core/src/handlers/send-agent-message.ts:16 is the `!ctx.sendAgentMessage` guard, and the handler really does validate only non-empty sessionId/message plus self-send. The finding fails on the third check -- the consequence. Its own load-bearing evidence is 'Our SchedulerTick automations create exactly the unwatched sessions the rule exists for, and they carry the tool', and that is false for the shipped default. Automation prompt actions create their session at packages/server-core/src/sessions/SessionManager.ts:18585 with `permissionMode: permissionMode || 'explore'`. `send_agent_message` is declared `safeMode: 'block'` (packages/session-tools-core/src/tool-defs.ts:1038), and packages/shared/src/agent/mode-manager.ts:2407-2422 denies every `mcp__session__*` tool absent from `getSessionSafeAllowedToolNames` (tool-defs.ts:1286-1293, which keeps only `safeMode === 'allow'`) for any mode that is not default/acceptEdits/auto/bypassPermissions (mode-types.ts:98-100 gate at mode-manager.ts:2160-2170). So an unattended SchedulerTick run in its default mode is already refused the tool -- enforcement one layer up from the handler, which is exactly false-positive shape #3 recorded in docs/superpowers/specs/2026-07-29-inert-worklist.md:108. The same gate blocks it in `dontAsk`, the mode this repo labels 'Unattended' (mode-manager.ts:2543). Two further scope points: our R27b scheduling primitive is session-scoped and delivers a scheduled prompt into the SAME session between turns (packages/session-tools-core/src/context.ts:428-446), so 'a scheduled-task run' has no unwatched-session counterpart on that path at all; and docs/superpowers/specs/2026-07-31-claude-coverage-map.md row 98 already carries the verdict WHITE / 'chuzhoy desktop-produkt' for this page. column5: If it did, Desktop starts exactly one catch-up run for the most recently missed time and discards anything older.
column6: On app start or wake, each task is checked for runs missed in the last seven days, and exactly one catch-up run fires for the most recently missed time.
column7: No catch-up of any kind. `SchedulerService.start()` aligns to the next minute boundary and then fires `setInterval(… , 60_000)`; a tick that did not happen because the app was closed is simply never emitted, and `grep -ai "catch-up\|catchup\|missedRun\|lastRun"` over `packages/shared/src/automations` and `packages/shared/src/scheduler` returns zero non-test hits. A daily 9am task on a machine that was off at 9am never runs that day.
column9: All three legs survive the challenge. (1) QUOTE VERBATIM: curl -sL of https://code.claude.com/docs/en/desktop-scheduled-tasks.md (HTTP 200, 11740 bytes) puts the sentence on line 74, character-for-character, in the '## Missed runs' section. The whole line was read: the surrounding sentences reinforce rather than reverse it -- 'Desktop checks whether each task missed any runs in the last seven days', 'A daily task that missed six days runs once on wake', 'Desktop shows a notification when a catch-up run starts'. Line 70 of the same page ('If your computer sleeps through a scheduled time, the run is skipped') is about the in-session tick, not about the wake sweep, and the Missed-runs section is what governs. The page is row 97 of scripts/claude-doc-pages.tsv, so it is a real Claude Code contract page, not a Codex/MCP page conflated in. (2) CITED LINE: packages/shared/src/scheduler/scheduler-service.ts start() spans :33-45. :34 is the re-entrancy guard `if (this.timer || this.alignmentTimer) return;` and the described mechanism is at :37-44 -- `msUntilNextMinute` alignment, then `setInterval(() => this.tick(), 60_000)`. Off by a line or two on the anchor, dead accurate on the substance: there is no immediate tick, no replay, no persisted cursor; the first tick lands at the next minute boundary. (3) CONSEQUENCE, verified separately from the identifier: the durable Nessy analogue of Desktop scheduled tasks is the Automations subsystem (this repo says so itself at docs/superpowers/specs/2026-07-26-r-queue-doc-verification.md:258 -- 'the DURABLE half of Claude's Desktop scheduled tasks mostly exists' in packages/shared/src/automations, with 'one catch-up run for the most recently missed time within seven days' named as part of the remaining gap, proposed as R31). Its scheduled trigger is packages/shared/src/automations/utils.ts:289 in matchesBasePredicate -- `return !!matcher.cron && matchesCron(matcher.cron, matcher.timezone)` -- and cron-matcher.ts:25-52 matches only whether the cron's nextRun falls inside the CURRENT minute window. No last-fired cursor is read anywhere on that path. Nothing upstream compensates: automation-system.ts:162 starts the scheduler and :396 only re-emits the tick onto the event bus; the history store (appendAutomationHistoryEntry, automations:getLastExecuted) is write-and-display only -- useAutomations.ts:62 hydrates lastExecutedAt purely for the 'last ran' label and no scheduling code reads it; retry-scheduler.ts is a webhook retry queue, unrelated; and grep -ain for powerMonitor over apps/electron/src/main and packages/server-core/src finds no OS wake/resume hook at all. So a daily 9am automation on a machine that was off at 9am does not run that day. NOT one of the nine dated owner decisions in 2026-07-29-inert-worklist.md section 3 (seatbelt wildcard, availableModels/isManagedModelAllowed, autoMode.classifyAllShell, ManagedDeliveryStateV1.drops, plugins/hooks-runtime.ts, SdkMcpServerConfig.required, SessionMirrorStore.delete, MirrorSessionKey.subpath, listSessionSummaries) -- and not a branding, subscription-flow or gateway product difference either. It is a recorded-but-OPEN product-surface gap, which is still a gap. TWO CORRECTIONS the finding needs, neither of which overturns it. First, the sibling-subsystem check does bite the wording: 'No catch-up of any kind' is overstated repo-wide, because packages/shared/src/sessions/cron-scheduler.ts + cron-store.ts + packages/server-core/src/sessions/session-cron-service.ts DO carry a lastFiredAt cursor, a cursorFor() helper and explicit catch-up prose (cron-scheduler.ts:121-131, cron-store.ts:198, sessions/index.ts:207). That tier delivers exactly one fire for an occurrence missed while the turn was busy and discards older ones because the cursor moves at delivery, not at enqueue (session-cron-service.ts:144-184). But that is the session-scoped Cron*//loop tier implementing scheduled-tasks.md:215, a DIFFERENT contract that forbids per-interval catch-up -- and session-cron-service.ts:9-16 explicitly documents why it is not SchedulerService. It is not the Desktop-Routines durable scheduler and does not survive an app restart in that sense, so it does not supply the behaviour this page specifies. Second, the finding's grep is scoped to only packages/shared/src/automations and packages/shared/src/scheduler; 'zero non-test hits' is true for those two directories but is not a repo-wide absence claim, and stating it as one is exactly how the sibling-subsystem trap fires. With the wording narrowed to the Automations subsystem, the divergence stands.

The whole line was read; the first sentence corroborates rather than reverses it — 'By default, scheduled tasks run against whatever state your working directory is in, including uncommitted changes. Enable the worktree toggle when creating the task to give each run its own isolated Git worktree, the same way [parallel sessions](/docs/en/desktop#work-in-parallel-with-sessions) work.' column9: All three refutation grounds were tested and none holds. (1) QUOTE — verbatim. curl -sL of env-vars.md puts the sentence at line 78, word for word. Read whole: line 78 is four sentences, and the remaining three only add caveats (a startup-only reader such as OpenTelemetry keeps its startup values; removing a variable does not unset it in a running session) — they do not reverse the conclusion. The page's own lines 89-98 give the four-scope table (user / project / local / managed) and lines 104-112 give the override-the-shell and re-apply-on-change semantics the finding restates, so the CLAIMED BEHAVIOUR is a fair reading, not an inflation. env-vars is row 101 of scripts/claude-doc-pages.tsv, so the citation is against a real Claude Code contract page. (2) CITED LINES — two of three exact. managed-policy.ts:359 is literally 'readonly env?: Readonly<Record<string, string>>'; project-config.ts:138 is literally the FORBIDDEN_SECTIONS line carrying 'env', 'environment'. validators.ts:521 is off by five lines (it is authType); the MCP stdio env record the finding means is at validators.ts:526. Not a product difference either — this is not a rename, not a dropped subscription flow, not gateway scoping. Two partial substitutes exist and neither closes it: apps/electron/src/main/shell-env.ts spawns the login shell and imports its environment at Electron startup, which answers the doc's stated MOTIVATION (they take effect no matter how claude was launched) but is macOS-only, skipped in dev mode, cannot set a variable absent from the profile, and cannot override one; and the network variables the docs single out as belonging in the env block are typed user-scope settings instead (NetworkProxySettings, config/types.ts:27), where refusing an env-block merge is a RECORDED security property (plans/2026-07-28-network-trust-chain.md Task 4). column5: Number of [subagent layers](/docs/en/sub-agents#let-subagents-spawn-their-own-subagents) allowed below the main conversation {/* min-version: 2.1.219 */}(default: 3).

column9: All three checks pass; the finding stands. (1) DOC - the sentence exists VERBATIM (exact substring match via python, not eyeballed) at line 280 of the curl'd https://code.claude.com/docs/en/env-vars.md, in the `CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_DEPTH` table row. Read WHOLE: the row is '{/* min-version: 2.1.217 */}Number of [subagent layers](...) allowed below the main conversation {/* min-version: 2.1.219 */}(default: 3). At the default, subagents can spawn their own subagents, and a subagent at the third layer can't spawn further; set `1` to turn nesting off. In v2.1.217 through v2.1.218, the default was 1, so a subagent couldn't spawn its own unless you raised the limit; v2.1.219 raised the default to 3. Accepts a positive whole number in plain digits; anything else is ignored, so the limit can be adjusted but not removed. Requires Claude Code v2.1.217 or later'. Nothing in the later sentences reverses the conclusion - they corroborate the claimed behaviour word for word, including that 1 is the nesting-off value. `env-vars` is a real Claude Code contract page in scripts/claude-doc-pages.tsv, not a Codex or platform page. (2) CODE - packages/pi-agent-server/src/orchestrator/spawner.ts:110 is exactly `export const DEFAULT_MAX_DEPTH = 1`, docblock :105-109 'Default child-session nesting depth: ONE level of delegation. Must stay in lockstep with `DEFAULT_PI_ORCHESTRATOR_CONFIG.depth`'. Enforcement is spawner.ts:513-520: `const depth = (args.depth ?? 0) + 1` then `if (depth > (cfg.maxDepth ?? DEFAULT_MAX_DEPTH)) return failure(..., `Subagent depth limit exceeded (${cfg.maxDepth ?? DEFAULT_MAX_DEPTH})`)`. Semantics match Claude's counting: main conversation spawns at depth 1 (allowed), a child spawning a grandchild computes depth 2 > 1 and is refused - i.e. exactly one subagent layer below the main conversation, which is Claude's `1` = nesting off. The mirror default is packages/shared/src/agent/pi-harness/harness-manifest.ts:107 `depth: 1` inside DEFAULT_PI_ORCHESTRATOR_CONFIG (the claim cites :106, which is the last comment line - a one-line citation drift, not a substantive error). Env override absent, checked NUL-safe with `grep -arn SPAWN_DEPTH .` over the whole repo (no --include filter, binary-safe): five files, ALL under docs/ (this sweep's own JSON/TSV/markdown plus 2026-07-26-r-queue-doc-verification.md). Zero readers in packages/, apps/ or scripts/, for either `CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_DEPTH` or a `NESSY_` equivalent. (3) CONSEQUENCE verified separately from the identifier, both directions. Layer UP: maxDepth reaches the spawner only via `maxDepth: config.orchestrator?.depth` (packages/pi-agent-server/src/index.ts:1279), and the single production seed - packages/server-core/src/sessions/SessionManager.ts:4152-4164 - populates contextSeed, sessionDepth, sessionIsFork, forkSubagent and tierModelMap and NEVER `depth`, so normalizePiOrchestratorConfig (harness-manifest.ts:233-234, `{ ...DEFAULT_PI_ORCHESTRATOR_CONFIG, ...input }`) falls back to 1 on every real session. Layer DOWN: proved positively with a control on the same rig - I RAN `bun test packages/pi-agent-server/src/orchestrator/spawner.test.ts -t depth` (7 pass, 0 fail). spawner.test.ts:537-546 'refuses a grandchild at the default depth but still admits a child' asserts child.status === 'done', grandchild.status === 'error' containing 'depth limit', started === 1; :549-554 'still allows a grandchild when the config raises the depth' passes maxDepth 2 and the identical grandchild spawn succeeds - the positive control; :532-535 pins both constants to 1. Sibling-subsystem check: this is the Pi orchestrator's own spawner, the default runtime (NESSY_FEATURE_PROVIDER_CLAUDE is off by default), and the depth gate is the only one on that path; the fork-cannot-fork rule is a separate UNCONDITIONAL flag (spawner.ts:96-98) rather than a depth derivative, so the subsystem is named correctly. column7: Truncation is a hard byte cut at 32 KiB with the overflow discarded — the trailing marker is a bare `[Output truncated to 32KB for the parent context.]` with no file path — and there is no env override (no `NESSY_TASK_MAX_OUTPUT_LENGTH`; 0 hits for TASK_MAX_OUTPUT_LENGTH repo-wide).
column9: All three checks confirm the finding. (1) The quoted sentence exists VERBATIM in env-vars.md, line 425, in the `TASK_MAX_OUTPUT_LENGTH` row. The whole line reads: "| `TASK_MAX_OUTPUT_LENGTH` | Maximum number of characters in [subagent](/docs/en/sub-agents) output before truncation (default: 32000, maximum: 160000). When truncated, the full output is saved to disk and the path is included in the truncated response |" — the first sentence supplies the default/maximum the claim cites and the second does not reverse it. (2) The cited code says exactly what was claimed: packages/pi-agent-server/src/orchestrator/subagent-tool.ts:24 `const OUTPUT_CAP_BYTES = 32 * 1024;` and :171-178 `truncateOutput` byte-cuts and appends the bare marker `[Output truncated to 32KB for the parent context.]` — no path, no disk write. Live call site is :236 inside `contentForResults`. (3) The consequence holds independently of the identifier. `TASK_MAX_OUTPUT_LENGTH` has 0 hits repo-wide outside the sweep's own data files (rg -a, so NUL-byte files were not skipped); there is no `NESSY_*` analogue; the cap is a module constant with no config or orchestrator-config path (the only `maxOutputBytes` in the repo is the workflow sandbox's, orchestrator/sandbox.ts:28, a different subsystem). column5: Claude wrote to the [auto memory](/docs/en/memory#auto-memory) index `MEMORY.md` and left it over one of its read limits: 200 lines or 25KB.
column6: A write that leaves the auto-memory index MEMORY.md over 200 lines or 25KB returns an error to the model naming the overflow, because everything past the limit is silently dropped on every subsequent load.
column7: We have the read limit (`MEMORY_LOAD_LINE_LIMIT = 200`) and we DO silently truncate at load (`readFileSync(...).split(/\r?\n/).slice(0, maxLines)`), but the write path (`appendMemory`) performs no post-write size check and returns no error or reminder — exactly the pre-v2.1.210 behaviour the page describes as the defect. There is also no 25KB byte limit and no frontmatter/HTML-comment exclusion.
column9: Tried all three refutation axes and none holds. (1) DOC VERBATIM: curl -sL https://code.claude.com/docs/en/errors.md (1679 lines) carries the quoted sentence word-for-word at :1437, opening the section '### Memory index is over its read limit'. Read the WHOLE line — it is three sentences and the other two REINFORCE rather than reverse: 'The write succeeded, but only the first 200 lines or 25KB, whichever comes first, load at the start of a session, so everything past the limit is dropped each time the index is read. Before v2.1.210, an over-limit index was silently truncated on the next load with no write-time signal.' The surrounding block adds the literal error text (:1440, naming line count and the 'Rewrite it to under 140 lines' remedy), a {/* min-version: 2.1.211 */} refinement that frontmatter and block-level HTML comments are stripped before measurement, 'Claude Code delivers the error to Claude after the write rather than printing it as a banner', and 'When Claude's write brings the file near a limit without crossing it, Claude Code returns a milder reminder to compact the index instead of this error.' :101 lists the error in the top-level index table. The page is row 102 of scripts/claude-doc-pages.tsv ('errors Error reference'), so it is a valid Claude contract citation, not a Codex or MCP page. (2) CITED CODE says what was claimed. memory-store.ts:8 is `export const MEMORY_LOAD_LINE_LIMIT = 200;` and :29-33 is readMemoryFile doing `readFileSync(filePath,'utf-8').split(/\r?\n/).slice(0, maxLines)` — a silent slice, no signal. remember.ts:39-49 is appendMemory: read existing, formatMemoryFile, write temp, rename, chmod — and :90-91 is `appendMemory(filePath, memory); return successResponse(`Saved memory to ${filePath}`);`. No measurement, no error, no reminder. (3) CONSEQUENCE verified separately from the identifier, one layer up and one layer down, including the sibling-subsystem trap. UP: `remember` is live and model-reachable (tool-defs.ts:981, safeMode 'block'). DOWN/SIBLING: there is a SECOND writer on a different subsystem — appendMemoryFile (memory-store.ts:122-132), reached by the renderer RPC path ChatDisplay.tsx:1557 -> dto.ts:519 `{type:'appendMemory'}` -> sessions.ts:564 -> :80 — and it has no post-write check either, so naming only the tool path understates it. Absence positively controlled with `rg -na` (NUL-byte-safe) for 'over its|read limit|left the memory|rewrite it to under|near a limit' across packages/ and apps/: zero memory-related hits, so neither the hard error nor the documented milder near-limit reminder exists. No byte cap exists anywhere on the memory path: the only *_MAX_BYTES in the subsystem is AUTO_MEMORY_CLEANUP_MAX_BYTES = 256*1024 (memory-cleanup.ts:33), a skip-guard in the scheduled dream pass (:125 leaves oversized files unchanged), not a 25KB load or write limit. No frontmatter or block-level HTML-comment exclusion: only the auto-marker `<!-- nessy:auto:YYYY-MM-DD -->` is stripped (stripAutoMemoryMarkers, memory-store.ts:159-163), and in the legacy path that strip happens in mergeMemoryContents AFTER the 200-line slice. NOT an owner decision: 2026-07-29-inert-worklist.md section 3's nine dated decisions are SEATBELT_TESTING_WILDCARD, availableModels/enforceAvailableModels, autoMode.classifyAllShell, ManagedDeliveryStateV1.drops, plugins/hooks-runtime.ts, SdkMcpServerConfig.required, SessionMirrorStore.delete, MirrorSessionKey.subpath/listSubkeys, and listSessionSummaries/listSessions — none touches memory limits. NOT a deliberate product difference either: this fork has a real auto-memory subsystem (remember tool + marker + scheduled cleanup), so the de-brand, the dropped Claude/ChatGPT subscription flows and the corporate gateway are all irrelevant here. Note for the collector: this substantially duplicates f103 (same defect cited from memory.md:386) and is adjacent to f092/f098/f104 (the missing 25KB load cap) — one fix closes all of them.

column5: Every entry in the subagent's [`tools` list](/docs/en/sub-agents#supported-frontmatter-fields) failed to match a usable tool, so Claude Code refused to launch the subagent: with no tools, it couldn't act.
column6: When every entry in a subagent's `tools` frontmatter list fails to match a usable tool, the spawn is refused with a diagnostic grouping the entries by cause, rather than launching a toolless subagent.
column7: `allowedTools()` filters the declared list against `disallowedTools` only and hands the result straight to the child restrictions. Unrecognised names, names not available to subagents, and names matching nothing in the session are all passed through unvalidated, and an empty result is not detected — the child launches with no usable tools and no error.
column9: Quote verified verbatim at errors.md:1400 (whole line read; no reversing second sentence). But the finding cites the WRONG LAYER, and its three-part description of our state is false at the layer that actually does the work. (1) The cited code, spawner.ts:296-298 `allowedTools()`, filters the declared list against `disallowedTools` only -- exactly as claimed -- yet errors.md:1406 explicitly carves that case OUT of the refusal: 'Omitting the `tools` field never triggers this refusal. If you leave the `tools` list empty, or `disallowedTools` removes every entry in it, Claude Code also skips the refusal and launches the subagent without tools.' So the one line cited as evidence is conformant, not divergent. (2) The layer that handles the doc's three groups is upstream: `resolveExplicitTools` / `buildPiRuntimeAgentDefinitions` (packages/pi-agent-server/src/orchestrator/runtime-agent-definitions.ts:92-126 and :129-179), called in production at packages/pi-agent-server/src/index.ts:1313 with the session's real tool set (`manifest.tools.map(t => t.binding.piName)` plus `manifest.deferredMcp.candidatePiNames`). It resolves each declared name exactly, case-insensitively, then via PI_RUNTIME_AGENT_TOOL_ALIASES. 'Unrecognized' -> pushed onto `unresolved` and `throw new Error('Unavailable runtime agent tool(s): ...')` at :122-124 (fail-closed, and STRICTER than Claude, which refuses only when ALL entries fail). 'Not available to subagents' -> SUBAGENT_UNAVAILABLE_TOOLS (:50) stripped at :125, and ORCHESTRATION_TOOLS (:33-40) withheld from a tool-less descriptor's ceiling. 'Matched no tools in this session' -> a recognized alias with no counterpart in this manifest is 'denied by omission' at :116-120. The host re-validates the arriving list against the pinned definition (packages/server-core/src/sessions/SessionManager.ts:10859, `runtime-agent-tool-unavailable:<tool>`) and re-filters it against `parentTools` at :10994. So 'unrecognised names, names not available to subagents, and names matching nothing in the session are all passed through unvalidated' is wrong on all three counts -- the textbook 'identifier unwired but consequence false because something upstream already handled it'. (3) Only a narrow residual survives: there is no 'Agent would be spawned with zero tools - refusing' refusal with entries grouped by cause (`grep -a` for 'zero tools'/'resolved to nothing' over all TS sources returns only an unrelated MCP test). A list whose entries all resolve to dropped entries yields `effectiveTools` = union with SUBAGENT_ALWAYS_AVAILABLE_TOOLS (runtime-agent-definitions.ts:83, :149) -- usually five task/report tools, occasionally empty -- and the spawn proceeds. That is Claude's own pre-v2.1.208 behaviour (errors.md:1408), and it is a missing diagnostic, not the unvalidated pass-through the finding describes. Not one of the nine dated owner decisions in 2026-07-29-inert-worklist.md section 3, and not a branding/product difference.

column5: Claude Code tests the pattern with `pgrep` before running `pkill` and refuses when its own process ID is in the result.
column6: A `pkill` whose pattern matches the agent's own process is refused before it runs; the pattern is probed with `pgrep` and the refusal is returned in the Bash tool result.
column7: `pkill` is only classified as a dangerous command that requires a permission decision — there is no self-PID probe. `pgrep` appears nowhere in the tool/permission path (only in build scripts and a shellguard corpus fixture), so in a mode that does not prompt, a matching pattern can terminate the agent process mid-turn.
column8: packages/shared/src/agent/core/pre-tool-use.ts:1751; packages/shared/src/agent/core/permission-manager.ts:46; grep -ra --include="*.ts" -ln "pgrep" . → no hit under packages/*/src runtime paths
column9: REFUTED on the second-sentence trap. (1) The quoted sentence IS verbatim at errors.md:1456 -- 'Claude Code tests the pattern with `pgrep` before running `pkill` and refuses when its own process ID is in the result.' But it is sentence 2 of a FOUR-sentence paragraph on one line, and sentence 3 reverses the scope the finding asserts: 'The check runs on Linux only; on macOS, `pkill` runs unmodified.' The CLAIMED BEHAVIOUR is stated unconditionally ('A `pkill` whose pattern matches the agent's own process is refused before it runs') -- that is not what the page says. Sentence 4 adds 'Before v2.1.214, the command ran, and a matching pattern killed the Claude Code session mid-turn', i.e. the claimed consequence is Claude Code's OWN shipped macOS behaviour today. (2) CLAIMED OUR STATE is factually accurate and I confirmed it: permission-manager.ts:46 lists 'kill','killall','pkill' in DANGEROUS_COMMANDS (read via isDangerousCommand at :393); pre-tool-use.ts:1751 lists pkill in AUTO_RISKY_BASH_PATTERNS; `grep -ra pgrep` over packages/ apps/ returns ZERO production hits -- every src hit is a test (packages/shared/src/agent/__tests__/codex-e2e.test.ts:89, packages/codex-agent-server/src/__tests__/runtime-manager.test.ts:12 comment, packages/server-core/src/sessions/SessionManager.process-supervisor.test.ts:89 which asserts killShell does NOT use pgrep/pkill) plus the corpus fixture packages/shared/tests/shellguard-corpus.test.ts:107,679. The finding's 'only in build scripts' is imprecise (they are test files) but directionally right. A non-prompting mode does exist: mode-manager.ts:2160-2161 'In bypassPermissions mode, all tools are allowed (no restrictions)'. (3) The CONSEQUENCE is what fails, and it fails on platform, not on identifier. Nessy Desktop's only LIVE release/publish CI jobs are macOS: .gitlab-ci.yml:179 `release-macos` and :396 `publish-macos-dev`. `release-win` (:250), `release-linux` (:292), `publish-win-dev` (:406) and `publish-linux-dev` (:416) are ALL commented out. Linux is a latent build target only (apps/electron/scripts/build-linux.sh, an AppImage block in electron-builder.yml whose own comment says 'codex: Linux support is paused'). On macOS -- the sole shipped platform -- Claude Code runs `pkill` unmodified per its own documentation, so our behaviour is IDENTICAL to the documented Claude behaviour and there is no divergence on the shipped surface. On Windows `pkill` is not a native command and the Claude check is Linux-only there too. Nothing upstream or downstream changes this either way: the macOS seatbelt would not contain a signal even if armed (bash-seatbelt.ts:100 emits `(allow process*)`), and it is currently a wildcard `(allow default)` by owner decision 2026-07-21 (inert-worklist s3 item 1 -- that decision is about sandbox containment, NOT about pkill, so it is not the recorded decision that covers this row). This is also NOT one of the nine dated owner decisions in 2026-07-29-inert-worklist.md s3, and NOT a de-brand or dropped-subscription product difference -- it is refuted purely because the doc's Linux-only scope excludes the platform we ship. Worth keeping only as a scoped latent note: if a Linux release job is ever uncommented, the divergence becomes real, and the place to implement it already exists -- pre-tool-use.ts:1186-1200 documents `removalCircuitBreaker` as the one floor 'NOT skipped by allow-all', which is the same shape a pkill self-PID floor would need.

column5: Fast mode is supported on Opus 5 and Opus 4.8. It is not available on Sonnet, Haiku, or other models.
column6: Fast mode applies to Opus 5 and Opus 4.8; Opus 4.7 is no longer served at fast speed and the API rejects fast-mode requests for it.
column7: `shouldEnableFastMode` matches the single literal `claude-opus-4-7` and nothing else, so it targets only the removed model and never fires for Opus 4.8 (which IS in our catalogue, models-pi.ts:92) or Opus 5. When FEATURE_FLAGS.fastMode is turned on, every request it modifies sets `body.speed='fast'` plus the `fast-mode-2026-02-01` beta header on a model the API now rejects, while the two supported models get no speedup at all.
column9: Doc sentence CONFIRMED verbatim at fast-mode.md:15. Code literal CONFIRMED at unified-network-interceptor.ts:496-499 (`model === 'claude-opus-4-7'`). The CONSEQUENCE is refuted on four independent counts. (1) Unreachable: `FEATURE_FLAGS.fastMode` (feature-flags.ts:182) is a hardcoded `false` literal - not a getter, no env override, no settings key. Repo-wide grep -a finds no `/fast` command, no `fastMode`/`fastModePerSessionOptIn` settings key, no CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_FAST_MODE / SKIP_FAST_MODE handling, and `shouldEnableFastMode` has exactly one caller and zero tests. The asserted harm ('every request it modifies sets body.speed=fast ... on a model the API now rejects') cannot occur in any build; it requires editing source and rebuilding. The claim's own 'When FEATURE_FLAGS.fastMode is turned on' concedes this. (2) Wrong layer - the interceptor no longer serves the Claude path at all. packages/shared/AGENTS.md:49 records it: the interceptor is Pi-only via Bun --preload, the Claude SDK spawns a native binary since 0.2.113, and it names 'fast-mode override' explicitly as deferred Phase-2 work. The doc page describes Claude Code's /fast toggle; the cited code is a dormant Pi-subprocess request rewriter, a sibling subsystem. (3) The third evidence citation is factually wrong. models-pi.ts:92 is a doc comment explaining that bare Bedrock IDs like `anthropic.claude-opus-4-8` are REJECTED by Bedrock and filtered OUT - it is not catalogue membership. (Opus 4.8 is in the catalogue, but at config/models.ts:133.) (4) 'the two supported models get no speedup at all' overstates: `claude-opus-5` does not exist anywhere in the fork (grep -a, zero hits), so half the asserted harm has no subject. Also note the doc's own next line (fast-mode.md:17) says Claude Code ITSELF 'treats Opus 4.7 as a fast mode model everywhere it decides whether fast mode is on' - matching 4.7 is not by itself contrary to upstream behaviour; only the absence of 4.8/5 would be, and that absence is inside dead code. Not one of the nine owner decisions in inert-worklist.md section 3 (checked; no fast-mode row). Both files landed in the single squashed fork-baseline commit 845cf0a4, so this is inherited upstream code, never a Nessy decision. Product-difference context also applies: NESSY_FEATURE_PROVIDER_CLAUDE is off by default and the fork targets a corporate gateway.

column5: **Skills and subagents** override by name: when the same name exists at multiple levels, one definition wins based on priority (managed > user > project for skills; managed > CLI flag > project > user > plugin for subagents).
column6: When a skill of the same name exists at more than one level, the USER-scope definition wins over the project-scope one (managed > user > project).
column7: Skill collisions are resolved by `scopeSpecificity`, which ranks project(3) > workspace(2) > global(1) > builtin(0) for every non-MCP capability kind including skills — the inverse of the documented skill order for the user-vs-project pair. A repo checking in `.nessy-agent/skills/deploy` silently shadows the user's own `deploy` skill; on Claude it would not. The surrounding comment cites mcp.md for the MCP arm only, so the skill arm appears unexamined.
column9: All three checks confirm the finding. (1) Quote is verbatim: features-overview.md line 193 reads '* **Skills and subagents** override by name: when the same name exists at multiple levels, one definition wins based on priority (managed > user > project for skills; managed > CLI flag > project > user > plugin for subagents).' The rest of that line ('Plugin skills are namespaced to avoid conflicts. See skill discovery and subagent scope.') does not reverse it, and skills.md:122 corroborates independently: 'When skills share the same name across levels, enterprise overrides personal, and personal overrides project. A skill at any of these levels also overrides a bundled skill with the same name.' (2) The cited code says what was claimed: packages/shared/src/capabilities/resolver.ts:863-869 scopeSpecificity returns project 3 / workspace 2 / global 1 / builtin 0, and applyCollisionPolicy (:2011, preference tuple :2038-2042, sort :2045-2051) sorts every non-MCP bucket -- skills included, bucket key is `${kind}\u0000${logicalName}` at :2017 -- by scopeSpecificity DESCENDING, so the project record wins the unqualified alias. The docblock at :1993-2010 cites mcp.md for the MCP arm only; no skills.md citation exists for the non-MCP arm, and no test covers the user-vs-project pair (resolver.test.ts:255-263 covers workspace-vs-plugin, :266-283 covers same-scope nessy-vs-portable). (3) The consequence is real, verified empirically and one layer down, not inferred. A throwaway probe test through createCapabilityResolver with two same-named skill records -- scope global and scope project -- returned: global key alias=false, project key alias=true. The alias is load-bearing downstream: base-agent.ts:2124-2126 builds skillsByAlias from `runtime.view.skills.filter(skill => skill.selectedAsUnqualifiedAlias)`, and :2345-2350 gates bare-name skill mention resolution on the same flag, so a bare `deploy` reference resolves to the project skill and the user's own is reachable only by its qualified key. Scope mapping is unambiguous: native-sources.ts:899-904 puts BOTH `~/.agents/skills` (portable, the direct analogue of `~/.claude/skills`) and `${CONFIG_DIR}/skills` (CONFIG_DIR = `~/.nessy-agent`, paths.ts:18-21) at scope 'global', while :996-1010 puts `<project>/.nessy-agent/skills` at scope 'project'. Not an owner decision: none of the nine dated decisions in 2026-07-29-inert-worklist.md section 3 concerns scope precedence (they are SEATBELT_TESTING_WILDCARD, availableModels, autoMode.classifyAllShell, ManagedDeliveryStateV1.drops, hooks-runtime.ts, SdkMcpServerConfig.required, and three SessionMirrorStore rows), and grepping the plans and the parity audit for a skill-precedence ruling returns nothing. Not a deliberate fork difference either: this is neither a subscription-flow drop, a gateway concern, nor a rename. The one refinement to the claim's wording: the losing record is not removed -- it stays enabled and addressable by qualified key, and an info-severity diagnostic capability.collision.unqualified-alias is emitted (:2055-2061) -- but the bare name, which is what a user or the model types, does go to the project definition, which is the inversion the doc forbids.

column5: For a skill you didn't write, set [`skillOverrides`](/docs/en/skills#override-skill-visibility-from-settings) in settings to do the same without editing its file.
column6: A settings key `skillOverrides` hides or narrows a skill you did not write, without editing the skill file.
column7: No reader anywhere in the source tree — the identifier appears only in two planning documents under docs/superpowers/. `disable-model-invocation` frontmatter IS supported (packages/shared/src/capabilities/types.ts), so the file-authored half of the mechanism exists and only the settings-side override is missing.
column9: All three checks confirm the divergence. (1) VERBATIM: curl of https://code.claude.com/docs/en/features-overview.md line 227 contains the quoted sentence exactly. The whole line is a two-sentence-plus footnote whose earlier half describes `disable-model-invocation: true` in frontmatter; the second half is the quoted sentence and does not reverse it. The linked target (skills.md:635-663) specifies the shape: `skillOverrides` is a record of skill name -> one of `on` / `name-only` / `user-invocable-only` / `off`, absent means `on`, written by `/skills` into `.claude/settings.local.json`, and since v2.1.199 `off` also hides the skill from Remote Control and Agent SDK command lists. Plugin skills are explicitly EXEMPT (`Manage those through /plugin instead`). (2) CITED STATE: the file-authored half is confirmed present -- `packages/shared/src/capabilities/types.ts:129` documents and declares `skillDisableModelInvocation`, parsed at `packages/shared/src/capabilities/native-sources.ts:296-298`, carried through `resolver.ts:1007-1009,1659-1661` and `views.ts:190-192`, and ENFORCED twice: `agent/core/prompt-builder.ts:405` filters the skill out of `<available_skills>` and `agent/base-agent.ts:2141` refuses a model-origin invocation of the same skill. The settings half has no Nessy reader. Note the claim's grep evidence line is incomplete: `grep -rail skilloverride` also hits `packages/pi-agent-server/dist/index.js`, `apps/electron/dist/resources/{pi-agent-server,session-mcp-server}/index.js`, `apps/electron/resources/{pi-agent-server,session-mcp-server}/index.js`, `node_modules/@anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk/{sdk.d.ts,sdk.mjs}` and several more docs/data files -- but every one of those is vendored Claude Agent SDK settings-schema text inside a build artifact, not a Nessy implementation. Zero hits under any `src/` tree (`grep -rn -a -i skilloverride packages/*/src apps/*/src` is empty). (3) CONSEQUENCE, verified separately from the identifier, one layer up and one down. UP -- every settings-side skill control we do have was checked and none reproduces the behaviour: `disableBundledSkills` (`config/bundled-skills-settings.ts`, `config/storage.ts:1337-1353`) is a bulk on/off for bundled skills, not per-skill and not a visibility ladder; the native-source `enabled` flag (`native-sources.ts:551,594` -> `resolver.ts:1595` `record.sourceEnabled !== false`) is set only on `kind === 'source'` records (MCP/api/local), never on `kind === 'skill'` records built by `skillRecords()` at `native-sources.ts:266-290`, so it cannot disable a skill; session selection (`resolver.ts:737-739`, fed at `server-core/src/bootstrap/storage-runtime.ts:859`) supplies `enabledSourceKeys` for `kind === 'source'` only and no production producer supplies `transientlyDisabledKeys`. DOWN -- `disableModelInvocation` reaches the runtime exclusively from SKILL.md frontmatter or a plugin skill declaration; nothing merges a settings layer into it. SIBLING-SUBSYSTEM CHECK (the `disallowed-tools` trap): the per-capability toggle `setCapabilityEnabled(pluginKey, capabilityId, enabled)` (`plugins/management-service-v2.ts:283`, `plugins/store.ts:266`, RPC `server-core/src/handlers/rpc/plugins.ts:94`, UI `PluginInfoPage.tsx:334-343`) is keyed by `pluginKey` and therefore covers PLUGIN skills only -- which is precisely the population Claude's own page exempts from `skillOverrides`. It is the `/plugin` equivalent, not the `skillOverrides` equivalent, so it does not refute the row. NATIVE skills (`skillRecords` over home `~/.claude|.nessy/skills`, the managed config dir, the workspace `skills/` dir, and project `.nessy-agent`/`.claude` skills dirs) have no enable/disable/visibility control in any settings layer or UI. VENDORED-SDK CAVEAT, checked and rejected as a refutation: `node_modules/@anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk/sdk.d.ts:4635` types `skillOverrides`, and `claude-agent.ts:305` passes `settingSources: ['user','project','local']`, so the SDK does read the settings files that could carry the key -- but `claude-agent.ts:1118` puts `Skill` in `disallowedTools`, skills reach the model through Nessy's own capability/prompt-builder path instead, and the Claude provider is off by default (`NESSY_FEATURE_PROVIDER_CLAUDE`). No Nessy-owned code path honours the key on any backend. NOT one of the nine dated owner decisions in `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-07-29-inert-worklist.md` section 3 (SEATBELT_TESTING_WILDCARD, availableModels/enforceAvailableModels, autoMode.classifyAllShell, ManagedDeliveryStateV1.drops, plugins/hooks-runtime.ts, SdkMcpServerConfig.required, SessionMirrorStore.delete, MirrorSessionKey.subpath/listSubkeys, listSessionSummaries/listSessions) -- none touches skill visibility. NOT a de-brand or dropped-subscription-flow difference: skill visibility is provider-neutral and the fork ships a full native skills subsystem.

column5: The first 200 lines or 25 KB of the `MEMORY.md` index loads at the start of every session.
column6: The MEMORY.md index load is capped by BOTH a line count and a byte size; we cap only lines, so a 200-line file with long lines loads unbounded into every session's context.
column7: `readMemoryFile` slices to `MEMORY_LOAD_LINE_LIMIT = 200` lines and applies no byte limit; no 25 KB (or any) size constant exists in the memory subsystem.

column9: All three checks pass. (1) Quote is VERBATIM. curl of https://code.claude.com/docs/en/glossary.md line 45 (section '### Auto memory') reads in full: 'Notes Claude writes for itself based on your corrections and preferences, stored per git repository under `~/.claude/projects/`. All worktrees of the same repository share one auto memory directory. The first 200 lines or 25 KB of the `MEMORY.md` index loads at the start of every session. Auto memory is the Claude-written counterpart to [CLAUDE.md](#claude-md), which you write.' Nothing later in the line reverses it. memory.md:384 states the same rule with more force ('Content beyond that threshold is not loaded at session start') and memory.md:390 scopes it ('This limit applies only to `MEMORY.md`. CLAUDE.md files are loaded in full regardless of length'), so the byte cap is a MEMORY.md-specific rule, not a general instruction-file rule. (2) Cited file:line is accurate. packages/shared/src/agent/memory/memory-store.ts:8 is `export const MEMORY_LOAD_LINE_LIMIT = 200;` and :29-32 is `readMemoryFile(filePath, maxLines = MEMORY_LOAD_LINE_LIMIT)` doing `readFileSync(filePath,'utf-8').split(/\r?\n/).slice(0, maxLines)` with no byte check. `grep -rna` (with -a, so NUL-byte files are not skipped) over packages/shared/src/agent/memory finds only AUTO_MEMORY_CLEANUP_MAX_BYTES = 256*1024 in memory-cleanup.ts (the scheduled rewrite pass's input guard, not a load cap) and RULE_PATTERN_EXPANSION_BYTE_LIMIT = 4MB in rule-matching.ts (glob expansion). No 25 KB constant exists anywhere in the memory subsystem. (3) Consequence verified separately, one layer up and one layer down, and it is WORSE than claimed rather than refuted. Layer down: readMemoryFile's two call sites are prompts/system.ts:455 (via loadMemoryPromptBlock) and capabilities/native-sources.ts:427 (an @import-discovery line scan, not a content load). Layer up: system.ts:453-455 reads `const memoryContext = capabilityContextPinned ? '' : loadMemoryPromptBlock(...)`, so the 200-line route is the LEGACY fallback only — AGENTS.md already records that the capability runtime is active on every normal send. The live route is: buildNativeCapabilityInventory registers `join(configDir,'MEMORY.md')` (and the session MEMORY.md) as `kind:'memory'` records via memoryFileRecords (native-sources.ts:909-916, :980-989); views.ts:218-219 puts them in `view.memory` with no size filter; base-agent.ts composePinnedCapabilityContext iterates `runtime.view.memory` and calls `runtime.materializer.readText(layer.resource)`; materializer.ts:169-185 does `readFileSync(contentPath)` and returns `content.toString('utf-8')` whole. The content is pushed verbatim into the pinned block that rides every session. So on the shipped path neither the 25 KB byte cap nor even the 200-line cap applies. Not a recorded owner decision: inert-worklist section 3's nine dated decisions are SEATBELT_TESTING_WILDCARD, availableModels/enforceAvailableModels, autoMode.classifyAllShell, ManagedDeliveryStateV1.drops, plugins/hooks-runtime.ts, SdkMcpServerConfig.required, SessionMirrorStore.delete, MirrorSessionKey.subpath/listSubkeys, and listSessionSummaries/listSessions — none touch memory loading. Not a deliberate fork difference either: this is not a Claude/ChatGPT subscription flow, not gateway-specific, and not a rename. The parity audit at :1672-1675 independently names 'a documented load limit (first 200 lines or 25 KB of `MEMORY.md`, whichever comes first, with frontmatter and HTML comments stripped before measurement)' as part of the auto-memory subsystem it found we had understated. The only inaccuracy in the finding is its mechanism sentence 'we cap only lines' — true of the legacy composer, false of the live one, which caps nothing.

column9: The doc sentence is verbatim (goal.md:106, whole line: '`stop`, `off`, `reset`, `none`, and `cancel` are accepted as aliases for `clear`. Running `/clear` to start a new conversation also removes any active goal.' - the second sentence does not reverse it), and all three cited file:lines say what was claimed (slash-command-menu.tsx:17 has no `goal` member; harness-tool-descriptor.ts:286 is `sessionBinding('goal', 'Goal')`; goal-service.ts:31-38 is `GoalCommand`). But the load-bearing assertion built on them - '`GoalCommand` is reachable only through the `mcp__session__Goal` tool binding', hence 'a user cannot set, inspect or clear a goal' - is false. There is a second, explicitly USER-sourced path that is not model-invocable at all: `PiHarnessRuntimeControlRequestV1` carries `goal_create`, `goal_replace`, `goal_cancel`, `goal_complete`, `goal_blocked` and `goal_resume` (packages/core/src/types/pi-harness-runtime.ts:346-351); they are validated in packages/shared/src/protocol/pi-harness-runtime.ts:295-328 (which also REJECTS a caller-supplied `source`, see its test at :65) and handled in packages/server-core/src/sessions/SessionManager.ts:3279-3324, where `goal_create`/`goal_replace` call `GoalService.execute` with `source: 'user', creator: 'desktop'` and then `schedulePiGoalContinuation`. That surface is wired the whole way out: RPC `sessions.ts:246` -> preload `apps/electron/src/preload/bootstrap.ts:214` (`controlPiHarnessRuntime`) -> renderer hook `apps/electron/src/renderer/hooks/useAgentPanel.ts:121-123` (`control`), already held by ChatDisplay.tsx:717. Inspection is wired too: `PiHarnessRuntimeSnapshotV1.goal` (pi-harness-runtime.ts:308) carries condition, status, budgets, accounting and `lastEvaluation.reason` - the exact data Claude's no-arg `/goal` status shows - and it is parsed for the renderer in packages/shared/src/protocol/pi-harness-runtime.ts. So a user-set, user-cleared goal is a first-class modelled concept here, not an agent-only one, and the goal loop itself (settlement evaluator via `runMiniCompletion`, continuation dispatch, budgets) is implemented at SessionManager.ts:3360-3400. This is exactly the repo's recurring false-positive shape: the identifier is genuinely absent, but the consequence is wrong because a sibling path already handles it. Secondary: the parity audit already records `/goal` as a *completion condition* under section 5's 'Minor, no row, listed for completeness' list (2026-07-25-nessy-claude-parity-audit.md:1722), so it is a triaged item, not an unnoticed gap.
